core_obligations: Name the six displayed elements Omega^+_B, Omega^+_C, Omega^+_A, Omega^-_B, Omega^-_C, Omega^-_A and record that the automorphism rho cyclically permutes the first three and the last three (proof lines 1488-1501).

Compute the first difference: Omega^+_B - Omega^-_C equals (q - q^{-1}) A times the displayed element (eq:need0), which is zero by the defining relations, so Omega^+_B = Omega^-_C; applying rho twice gives Omega^+_C = Omega^-_A and Omega^+_A = Omega^-_B (proof lines 1502-1517).

Compute the second difference: Omega^+_B - Omega^-_A equals (q - q^{-1}) C times the displayed element (eq:need02), which is zero by the same relations, so Omega^+_B = Omega^-_A; applying rho twice gives Omega^+_C = Omega^-_B and Omega^+_A = Omega^-_C (proof lines 1518-1532).
Conclude that all six elements coincide, which defines the common element Omega named in the statement (proof lines 1533-1539).
proof_roadmap: Reduce the six coincidences to two differences by exploiting the cyclic symmetry rho (proof lines 1488-1501).
Evaluate each of the two differences as a scalar multiple of a defining relation, and propagate the resulting equalities around the cycle with rho (proof lines 1502-1539).
difficulty_reason: The lemma concerns the universal Askey-Wilson algebra and states that six explicit words of length three in A, B, C, with their quadratic and linear corrections, all define the same element, which the author names Omega (statement lines 1450-1485). The proof does not expand the products: it isolates two differences, computes each as an explicit scalar multiple of a quantity that vanishes by the defining relations, and then propagates the equalities around the cycle using the automorphism rho, giving all six coincidences from two verifications (proof lines 1488-1532). The content is in the reduction: recognising that rho permutes the six elements in two 3-cycles is what makes the computation finite, and the two displayed differences are then each identified with a defining relation. The single reference to another labelled item is the definition of the algebra's relations. H2.
